To keep data inside your network, point `base_url` at a gateway you run (a LiteLLM proxy, a Bedrock or Azure OpenAI gateway in your VPC, Ollama or vLLM on an internal host) and use `api_key_env` for the gateway credential. `llm doctor` shows the host so a reviewer can check it. liter-llm 2.2.2 and later refuse HTTP redirects: a gateway that answers 307 or 308 surfaces as a provider error and the prompt is never re-sent to the redirect target (`TestRedirectsAreNotFollowed`). Only point `base_url` at a host you trust. `base_url` must not embed credentials or a query string (`AR9L0`). The default endpoint (used only when `provider` is `openai` or empty and no `base_url` is set) is `https://api.openai.com/v1`. A key is sent only as an `Authorization: Bearer` header to that host, and only over `https` unless the host is loopback. `base_url`, `allow_network` and `api_key_env` are honoured only from user scope (see the trust rule above).

Model-side retention and training terms are the provider's; check them before sending transcripts that contain private code.

##### Amazon Bedrock

A `bedrock/...` model is signed with AWS credentials, resolved through the AWS SDK's default chain for **every** command that calls a model (`judge`, `eval`, `verifiers`, `review`, `improve`, `search`): environment variables, `AWS_PROFILE` and the shared config (SSO and assume-role profiles included), web identity (`AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE`), and container and instance roles. A Bedrock API key (`AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`) or a key pair already in the environment is used as it is. The SDK's credential cache renews temporary credentials before they expire, ai-rulez puts the current keys where liter-llm reads them before each call (calls in flight finish first), and a call refused as unauthenticated renews the credentials and is tried once more, so a run longer than a session does not fail halfway. The region comes from `AWS_REGION`, `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` or the `AWS_PROFILE` profile, and the egress host is `bedrock-runtime.<region>.amazonaws.com`. A Claude 5.x model on Bedrock takes no `temperature`: it is left out of the request up front, not retried after a 400.

##### Cost controls

Set `max_cost_usd`, `max_tokens` and `max_calls` for any feature that loops. Use `ai-rulez llm estimate <file>` to see what a prompt costs first (tokens are estimated at one per three UTF-8 bytes, which overestimates English text and holds for CJK). Prices come from liter-llm's embedded model catalog (`GetModelInfo` and `CompletionCostWithCache`, with context tiers and cache-read rates), which is approximate and only for budget estimates; `internal/pricing` adds a few fail-closed floors (see "Price floors"). Set `price_input_per_mtok` / `price_output_per_mtok` for anything else. Cost in responses is an estimate from that table, not a bill.

#### liter-llm

ai-rulez reaches every provider through [liter-llm](https://github.com/xberg-io/liter-llm), a Rust client with one interface for 174 providers (`provider/model` names, keys from the provider's environment variable). Its Go module is `github.com/xberg-io/liter-llm/packages/go/v2`, a cgo wrapper over the Rust library `libliter_llm_ffi`. It is a normal dependency of the root module and the only provider backend: there is no build tag, no nested module and no hand-written HTTP client. An OpenAI-compatible gateway, Ollama or vLLM is a `base_url`; liter-llm keeps a named provider's own transform (Gemini, Vertex, Bedrock, Anthropic, Azure) under it and falls back to a generic OpenAI-compatible one only for an unlisted provider, stripping the `provider/` prefix from the model it sends.

##### What liter-llm does and what ai-rulez keeps

| Responsibility | Owner | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Providers, routing by `provider/model`, wire formats, auth headers | liter-llm | `client.go` builds a typed `ChatCompletionRequest` |
| Chat, embeddings, structured output (`response_format`) | liter-llm | JSON-schema output is native on OpenAI and Anthropic (upstream #265) |
| Streaming, rate limits, in-flight limits, cooldown, tracing, cost tracking | liter-llm provides them | unused: ai-rulez makes sequential calls and keeps its own accounting |
| Retries, jittered backoff, `Retry-After` | liter-llm (`max_retries`) | `classify` carries a reported `Retry-After` onto `llm.Error` |
| Error taxonomy (typed variants, status, transient flag) | liter-llm | `classify` maps each variant sentinel to an `llm.Error` kind |
| Usage: prompt, completion, total, reasoning and cached tokens | liter-llm | right, including Gemini thinking tokens from 2.2.0 (#253) and Gemini and Anthropic cache accounting (#254, #255); `usageOf` charges the largest of the reported figures |
| Price catalog, `GetModelInfo`, context tiers, cache-read rate | liter-llm | `internal/pricing` calls it first; floors only where the catalog has no row (below) |
| Per-response cost | partly | the Go binding has `CompletionCostWithCache` only; `Pricing.Cost` applies a `price_*_per_mtok` override first |
| Token counting | liter-llm provides `CountTokens`, but it downloads a tokenizer from the network on first use and fails for Gemini | not used: `internal/tokens` stays (offline, deterministic cl100k_base counts for reports; a conservative byte estimate for the spend gate) |
| Budget | ai-rulez policy | liter-llm's budget is USD-only and charges after the fact; ours reserves the worst case on cost, tokens and calls and fails closed |
| Response cache | ai-rulez policy | outside the repository, HMAC-authenticated per user (liter-llm's cache is in-memory or OpenDAL) |
| Network gate, trust model (user-scope-only keys), routing/key check, dry run, judge, prompt redaction, `AR9L0` validation | ai-rulez policy | `gate.go`, `trust.go`, `redact.go`, `config.go` |
| Response size limit | liter-llm (cap: ai-rulez) | the cap is passed as `max_response_bytes` (32 MiB) through `lit.CreateClientWithOptions`; the body is refused while it is read |
| Redirect refusal | liter-llm | refused since v2.2.2; a 307/308 surfaces as a provider error, see "Data egress" |

##### Price floors

`GetModelInfo` is the price source. `internal/pricing` consults its own table only for a model the catalog has no entry for: the short names `haiku`, `sonnet` and `opus` that eval cases use, and the `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` and `claude-opus` families (upstream #262, still missing in v2.2.3). It also reduces a Bedrock model id to the model it names (the `global.`, `us.`, `eu.`, `apac.` ... inference-profile prefix, the `anthropic.`/`amazon.` vendor prefix, the `-v1:0` revision and a trailing date) before the catalog and floor lookup, and drops a provider prefix before the lookup, since `gemini/`, `google_ai/` and `vertex_ai/` names are not found by the catalog (#260). The catalog now matches a model only on its exact name, so an unlisted realtime, audio, tts or transcribe variant is unpriced rather than silently charged at its base model's rate (#260). Each correction carries a `TODO(liter-llm#NNN)` and is deleted when the catalog covers it. A model nothing prices is unpriced, so a cost limit refuses it unless you set `price_input_per_mtok` and `price_output_per_mtok`; a paid model the catalog lists at 0/0 is unpriced too, because `GetModelInfo` reports it as not `PriceKnown` (#276). The price source is `literllm-<version>+floors-<revision>` (`floorsRevision` is `3`) and is part of the cache identity.

##### Shims that remain

Each is marked `TODO(liter-llm#NNN)` in the code.

- `internal/llm/client.go`: `scrub` removes a key-shaped token or a URL query a provider can still echo (#259, still missing in v2.2.3); `needsMaxCompletionTokens` sends `max_completion_tokens` to a reasoning model behind a `base_url` (#264, partial: liter-llm renames the field for its own openai and azure providers only).
- `internal/pricing/pricing.go`: the floors for the Claude families and the short names (#262); `bare()` drops a provider prefix before the lookup (#260).

##### Linking and distribution

The binding is cgo over a Rust library, so a build needs `CGO_ENABLED=1`, a C toolchain and the native library. What links depends on who builds:

- **Contributors** run `go build ./...`, `go test ./...` and `golangci-lint` with nothing to set up. The binding's module ships the shared library for every platform in its own `.lib/<platform>/` directory and its cgo directives point there with an absolute rpath, so the result runs on the machine that built it. That binary is not portable and nobody should ship it.
- **Release builds** link the **static** archive (`libliter_llm_ffi.a`), which makes each binary one self-contained executable with no sidecar library and no cache directory. `scripts/setup-liter-llm.sh` downloads the release asset for the version pinned in `go.mod`, verifies its `.sha256` sidecar (it fails closed), extracts only `libliter_llm_ffi.a` and prints `CGO_LDFLAGS=-L<dir>`; a `-L` that comes first on the link line and holds no shared library makes `-lliter_llm_ffi` resolve to the archive. `task build` and `task test:release` do this, `scripts/package-release.sh` checks the result with `otool -L` / `ldd` (no `liter_llm` dependency), and CI sets it up with `.github/actions/setup-liter-llm`.

A cgo `#cgo LDFLAGS` shim inside the repository cannot replace the environment variable: the binding's own `-L` and `-lliter_llm_ffi` come first on the link line and resolve to the shared library the module ships, so the binary keeps a load command for it (checked on macOS arm64; `-Wl,-dead_strip_dylibs`, which would drop it, is not allowed in `#cgo` flags). That is why `scripts/setup-liter-llm.sh` supplies the static archive through `CGO_LDFLAGS` rather than an in-repo cgo shim.

Verification history for liter-llm (the current pin is v2.3.0; earlier platform checks retain their tested versions):

| Platform | Result | Verified on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| macOS arm64 | static link; `internal/llm` and `internal/evals` tests, race checks on `internal/llm` and `llm doctor` pass, and the binary has no load command for the shared library | v2.3.0 |
| macOS arm64 | static link; full Go tests, race checks and a live OpenAI smoke test pass | v2.2.4 |
| Linux arm64 (glibc, Debian bookworm container) | release archive and smoke test pass; static liter-llm link, `ldd` lists libm, libgcc_s and libc only; highest required symbol is `GLIBC_2.34` | v2.2.4 |
| Linux x86_64, macOS x86_64 | native release builds and smoke tests passed in the [v5.3.0 publish run](maintainers/release.md#platform-matrix) | v2.2.3 |
| Windows x86_64 | archive packaging and smoke tests passed in the [v5.3.0 publish run](maintainers/release.md#windows); packaging can fall back to `liter_llm_ffi.dll` beside `ai-rulez.exe` when static linking fails | v2.2.3 |
| Windows arm64, Linux musl | liter-llm v2.2.3 now ships `windows-aarch64` and `linux-*-musl` assets (#267 closed), and its release workflow builds and tests each; ai-rulez has not linked or verified them, and its release matrix stays the five platforms above (Linux glibc only; musl-based images are unsupported) | not verified |

Binary size grows by about 35 MB per platform. The release workflow, glibc floor and the wrappers (npm, PyPI, Homebrew) are described in [maintainers/release.md](maintainers/release.md).

##### Licensing

liter-llm is MIT licensed (Copyright 2026 Kreuzberg, Inc.). The Go module is a wrapper around a Rust library whose dependency tree carries other licenses (its `deny.toml` allows Apache-2.0, MIT, BSD, ISC, Zlib, MPL-2.0, OpenSSL, among others), and its provider table is derived from LiteLLM's (MIT, attribution in liter-llm's `ATTRIBUTIONS.md`). Every release binary now bundles that code: ship the MIT notice and the third-party notices of the library with it.

Version pin: `github.com/xberg-io/liter-llm/packages/go/v2 v2.3.0` in `go.mod`. v2.2.0 or later is required for exact Gemini thinking-token accounting (`module_test.go` pins that floor).

##### Testing

The `internal/llm` tests run the real liter-llm client against local `httptest` servers: no network and no key. With a `base_url` liter-llm keeps the named provider's transform, so the Gemini (native and Vertex) and OpenAI request and usage mappings are asserted offline against a local server (`TestProviderTransformIsKeptWithABaseURL`); Bedrock is liter-llm's own tests' job. The live tests (`AI_RULEZ_LIVE_LLM=1`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`) cover Gemini end to end and are not part of PR CI; the `live-llm` job in `.github/workflows/live.yml` runs `go test ./internal/llm/... ./internal/evals/...` on `workflow_dispatch` and a weekly schedule. It needs the `GEMINI_API_KEY` repository secret (and optionally `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`, unused by the current tests), writes its transcripts to `AI_RULEZ_LIVE_OUT` and uploads them with the test log as an artifact.

Verified live on 2026-10-10 against liter-llm v2.2.3: `AI_RULEZ_LIVE_LLM=1` with `GEMINI_API_KEY`, chat model `gemini-2.5-flash-lite` and embedding model `gemini-embedding-001`; `go test ./internal/llm/... ./internal/evals/...` passes. Thinking-token settlement charged the reply's reported `total_tokens` (prompt 35, completion 414). That run also exposed a live-only test bug, since fixed: `TestLiveBudgetMaxCallsAndUnknownPriceWithCostCap` used a priced model for its unknown-price branch, so the branch never exercised an unpriced model.

On 2026-10-16, the statically linked v2.2.4 build passed the full Go suite, race checks and a live OpenAI smoke test. On 2026-10-20, the statically linked v2.3.0 build passed the `internal/llm` and `internal/evals` tests, race checks on `internal/llm` and `llm doctor` on macOS arm64; the other platforms are verified by the release workflow.

#### Using it from a feature

```go
lc, err := cfg.ResolvedLLM()            // cfg is the loaded *config.Config; env overrides applied
if err != nil { return err }
client, err := llm.New(lc, llm.Options{ConfigDir: cfg.ConfigDir})
if err != nil { return err }            // AR9L0; a disabled network surfaces on the first call
defer client.Close()

v, err := llm.Judge(ctx, client, rubric, transcript)   // v.Score in [0,1], v.Rationale
```

`llm.Judge` uses structured output at temperature 0 (omitted for an OpenAI reasoning model, which rejects any temperature but its default, for a Claude 5.x model, when `AI_RULEZ_LLM_TEMPERATURE=omit` is set, and, after one retry, once a provider answers HTTP 400 about `temperature`) and `llm.JudgePromptVersion` as the cache version. It asks for at least `llm.DefaultJudgeCompletionTokens` (2048) completion tokens, because a reasoning model spends its thinking out of that budget before the verdict (`JudgeOptions.MinCompletionTokens` raises it). Change the judge prompt or schema and bump that constant. The transcript is sent as data between two marker lines that carry a token derived from the request's own content (so the transcript cannot predict or close it), and the system prompt tells the model to ignore instructions inside it. The reply must be exactly one JSON object with both `score` (in [0,1]) and `rationale`; anything else is a provider error, and a reply that fails that check is never written to the cache (a cached one is treated as a miss). Before sending, the rubric and transcript are scanned for secret-looking text (bearer tokens, `sk-...`, `AKIA...`, `api_key=...`, and every credential shape the security scan `AR001` recognises, such as `AIza...`, `ghp_...`, `xoxb-...` and private key blocks); `Judge` refuses when it finds any, and `llm.JudgeWith(..., llm.JudgeOptions{RedactSecrets: true})` sends them masked instead. The scan is a pattern match, not a guarantee. A feature must treat `errors.Is(err, llm.ErrNetworkDisabled)` as "refuse with a clear message" and `llm.ErrDryRun` as "skipped". In tests use `llm.NewFake()` (deterministic, no network) and `llm.Wrap(fake, cfg, opts)` to get the real middleware around it.

## Performance

Source: https://goldziher.github.io/ai-rulez/performance/

How ai-rulez is benchmarked, how a regression is caught, and what the optimization passes changed.

#### Running the benchmarks

Every benchmark that reads a project builds a synthetic one in a temporary directory
(`internal/testutil.BuildBenchTree`): rules, context, skills, agents and commands with frontmatter and prose, plus
a git repository when the code under test asks git questions. Nothing touches the network.

| Size   | Content files | Runs by default |
| ------ | ------------- | --------------- |
| small  | 10            | yes             |
| medium | 200           | yes             |
| large  | 2000          | with `AI_RULEZ_BENCH_LARGE=1` |

```bash
task test:benchmark                 # every benchmark, small and medium
task test:benchmark:large           # adds the 2000-file project, one iteration each
go test ./internal/lint -run '^$' -bench RunFull -benchmem -cpuprofile cpu.out
go tool pprof -top -cum cpu.out
```

The repository-index benchmarks build a synthetic monorepo instead (`internal/testutil.BuildMonorepo`): every scope
holds an `AGENTS.md`, a `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and a `.claude/rules/<name>.md`, and the rest of the files
are small sources. The default run covers 100, 1000 and 5000 files over 10, 100 and 500 scopes (a shape needs four
files per scope); `AI_RULEZ_BENCH_LARGE=1` adds 20000 files, which take seconds to write, and moves the
`Resolve`, `Within` and `mcp` query benchmarks to that size.

| Package | Benchmarks |
| ------- | ---------- |
| `internal/parser` | `ParseFrontmatter` (no/small/rich/CRLF/long body), `ParseFrontmatterBatch` |
| `internal/tokens` | `Estimate`, `Count` (cl100k and byte ratio, prose and long-line input) |
| `internal/config` | `LoadConfig`, `LoadSkillResourcesContext` (one installed skill of 1, 100 and 2000 files), `LoadSkillResourcesCatalog` (200 skills) |
| `internal/repoindex` | `Build` (git listing and directory walk), `BuildPreListed`, `ListFiles`, `Resolve`, `Within` on synthetic monorepos |
| `internal/includes` | `LoadWithLocalInclude` |
| `internal/lint` | `LoadTree`, `RunFull`, `Analyzers` (each analyzer alone), `SecretScan` (`DetectSecret`, `RedactSecrets`, `ScanText`), `SecretScanLongLine`, `SecretScanCustomPatterns`, `RunSkillTree`, `AnalyzerSelection`, `NumberedPrefixExists`, `ScannerStage` (stage listing, digest and cache key of an external scanner over 50 and 500 skills) |
| `internal/contentlock` | `Compute`, `BuildAndCompare` (lock digest, then verify) |
| `internal/lockfile` | `SaveLoad` |
| `internal/generator` | `Generate` (full and idempotent no-op), `GeneratePresets` (2, 10 and every preset), `GenerateLLMsTxt`, `Clean` (remove and dry run), `CheckDrift`, `SecretGate` (plain and `-memo`, the context `generate` runs under) |
| `internal/review` | `Score` (collect and score), `Calibrate` |
| `internal/mcp` | `ProjectTools` (tool dispatch), `SkillServer` (catalog build, `search_skills`, `load_skill`), `DiscoveryCatalog` (catalog build with repository discovery on a monorepo), `RepositoryQueries` (`find_skill` and `find_context` with a path or scope) |
| `internal/verifiers` | `RegexFiles` |
| `cmd/commands` | `Lock` (write and check), `PublishDryRun` (bundle, agent-plugins, ard), `OKF` (export, validate) |

#### Regression tracking

CI does not compare against a number recorded on another machine. The `Benchmarks` job checks out the full history
and runs `scripts/bench.sh --compare`, which measures the base revision and `HEAD` on the same runner, in the same job:

1. It picks the base: the merge base with the default branch, or the parent commit when `HEAD` is on it (`--compare REF`
   or `BENCH_BASE` overrides it).
2. It builds the test binary of each package of a curated subset at both revisions (benchmarks that start no process
   and do not fsync, so they measure the code and not the machine; a package that does not build at the base is skipped
   with a notice).
3. It takes `BENCH_COUNT` samples (6) of each benchmark per revision, interleaved base, head, head, base, ..., so a
   machine that warms up or is throttled favors neither.
4. It compares the medians and runs a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test on the samples, the test `benchstat` uses.

A benchmark fails the job only when it is both more than `BENCH_THRESHOLD` percent slower (20) and different at
`BENCH_ALPHA` (0.05). A slowdown that is not significant is printed as `slower, not significant`, and a run with
fewer than 5 samples is refused, because it cannot reach the significance level. The large synthetic sizes stay out of
the subset; they run only with `AI_RULEZ_BENCH_LARGE=1`. The rest of the benchmarks run once in the job
(`task test:benchmark:smoke`, `-benchtime=1x`) to prove they still run.

```bash
task test:benchmark:regression                    # HEAD against the merge base, on this machine
scripts/bench.sh --compare origin/main            # the same, with an explicit base
BENCH_THRESHOLD=10 BENCH_COUNT=10 scripts/bench.sh --compare HEAD~3
```

When a run flags a benchmark you believe is noise, run it again locally with more samples
(`BENCH_COUNT=12`); a real regression stays significant. The job runs with `shell: bash` (so `pipefail` holds), and
uploads `bench-subset.txt`, the head samples. A change that intentionally makes a benchmark slower is not overridden by
a file: say so in the pull request and rerun the job; a maintainer can merge over a failure that the table explains.

`scripts/bench-baseline.txt` and `scripts/bench.sh` without an argument remain as a fallback for a developer machine:
the script compares `HEAD` with the committed file, but only when it was recorded on the same CPU model (the `cpu:` line
of the output), and otherwise warns and exits 0. Refresh it with `scripts/bench.sh --update` (`task
test:benchmark:baseline`). CI does not read it.

#### Monorepo index

`internal/repoindex` indexes the skills, instruction files, rules, agents and commands a repository keeps at any
depth (`mcp --serve-skills --discover-skills`). The numbers below are a cold build: the file listing, the
classification of every path, one read per item for its description and hash, and the grouping into scopes. They
come from `go test -bench` on the synthetic monorepo described above, 5 iterations per row, on a 4-vCPU Intel Xeon
2.1 GHz virtual machine with a slow file system for creating files. Compare rows with each other, not with
your machine or with the CI runners.

Cold `Build`, in ms (B/op in MB), by files and scopes. `git` lists files with `git ls-files`; `walk` is the fallback
in a directory that is not a repository.

| Files | Scopes | Items | git | git B/op | walk | walk B/op |
| ----- | ------ | ----- | --- | -------- | ---- | --------- |
| 100 | 10 | 30 | 11.1 | 1.3 | 5.9 | 0.9 |
| 1000 | 10 | 30 | 14.7 | 1.8 | 9.8 | 1.4 |
| 1000 | 100 | 300 | 25.0 | 5.3 | 22.8 | 5.3 |
| 5000 | 10 | 30 | 19.1 | 3.7 | 15.2 | 3.0 |
| 5000 | 100 | 300 | 47.4 | 7.2 | 51.3 | 8.5 |
| 5000 | 500 | 1500 | 78.2 | 23.3 | 89.7 | 25.0 |
| 20000 | 10 | 30 | 34.1 | 17.4 | 41.7 | 9.0 |
| 20000 | 100 | 300 | 51.4 | 23.7 | 88.5 | 14.8 |
| 20000 | 500 | 1500 | 129.1 | 49.8 | 202.2 | 37.9 |

The cost has two parts. The listing grows with the files: 36 ms for `git ls-files` on 20000 files and 67 ms for the
walk (`ListFiles`). Reading the items grows with their number, about 20-35 us each (a stat, a read, a YAML parse of
the frontmatter, a SHA-256): with the listing supplied (`BuildPreListed`) 20000 files take 4.1 ms for 30 items, 13.3 ms
for 300 and 35.7 ms for 1500. Classification costs about 0.2 us per file and is not a factor.

Queries on the built index are microseconds:

| Operation (20000 files) | ns/op | B/op | allocs/op |
| ----------------------- | ----- | ---- | --------- |
| `Resolve` of a path six directories deep, 10 / 100 / 500 scopes | 2400 / 2300 / 2300 | 2128 | 8 |
| `Within` a leaf scope | 9600 | 968 | 6 |
| `Within` the root, recursive (1500 items) | 371000 | 614344 | 16 |

`Resolve` walks the ancestors of the path and looks each up in a map, so it does not depend on the number of scopes.

Through the MCP server, the catalog build with discovery on (`BenchmarkDiscoveryCatalog`, 20000 files) is the sum of
the index build, reading every served skill directory, and the security scan of every item (`lint.ScanServed` for
skills, the index `Screen` for instruction files, rules and agents):

| Scopes | Items | Catalog build, median of 5 | B/op | allocs/op |
| ------ | ----- | -------------------------- | ---- | --------- |
| 10 | 30 | 65 ms | 22.1 MB | 130k |
| 100 | 300 | 291 ms | 58.8 MB | 363k |
| 500 | 1500 | 1220 ms | 220.8 MB | 1.30M |

The index cache (`[mcp] index_cache`, `docs/mcp-server.md#the-index-cache`) removes most of that on a later start.
`BenchmarkDiscoveryCatalogCache` starts the same server three ways on the 20000-file monorepo: `off` keeps no cache,
`cold` starts with an empty cache and writes it, `warm` starts with the cache of an earlier start, over files whose
modification time is an hour old (a file modified in the two seconds before a save is read again). Mean of 5 starts,
same machine as above:

| Scopes | Items | off | cold (fills the cache) | warm | warm B/op | warm vs off |
| ------ | ----- | --- | ---------------------- | ---- | --------- | ----------- |
| 10 | 30 | 48.9 ms | 58.1 ms | 22.7 ms | 5.5 MB | -54% |
| 100 | 300 | 316.8 ms | 292.4 ms | 53.5 ms | 11.3 MB | -83% |
| 500 | 1500 | 1251 ms | 1450 ms | 106 ms | 37.3 MB | -92% |

A cold start with the cache on costs what a start without it does, plus the write of the index file (the 10 and 500 scope
rows differ from `off` by run-to-run noise as much as by that write). A warm start no longer reads, hashes or scans an
unchanged item: what remains is the file listing, one `stat` per candidate, the configuration load and reading the
served skill directories. The live refresh of the index pays the warm cost per change, not the cold one.

Most of that is the security scan, not the index (before the fifth pass about 90% of a build; `Build` alone is 129 ms at 500 scopes). Queries over the
in-memory transport (`BenchmarkRepositoryQueries`, one sample each; every call also pays about 0.5 MB and 0.3 ms of
protocol overhead, the same as `search_skills`):

| Query | 10 scopes | 100 scopes | 500 scopes |
| ----- | --------- | ---------- | ---------- |
| `find_skill` with a task | 0.59 ms | 0.76 ms | 1.71 ms |
| `find_skill` with a task and a path | 0.51 ms | 0.71 ms | 1.73 ms |
| `find_skill` with a scope, recursive | 0.38 ms | 0.67 ms | 1.52 ms |
| `find_context` with a path | 0.51 ms | 0.54 ms | 0.46 ms |
| `find_context` with a task and a path | 0.33 ms | 0.34 ms | 0.32 ms |
| `find_context` with a scope, recursive | 0.76 ms | 0.82 ms | 1.09 ms |

`find_skill` ranks the whole served catalog, so it grows with the skills (500 at most, the discovery cap);
`find_context` only ranks the scopes that apply to the path.

`TestBuildOfAMonorepoStaysFast` fails when a cold build of 5000 files over 100 scopes takes more than 2 seconds (it
measures 50-70 ms); it is skipped under `-short` and the race detector.

What a cache would save: the index build itself is 5-130 ms even at 20000 files, so caching only the listing and
the item summaries (the proposal's phase 3) removes at most that. The larger cost in the server is the per-item
security scan, which a cache keyed by content hash would also skip.

#### Installed skill bundles

Installing or serving a skill reads its whole directory (`config.LoadSkillResourcesContext`): every file besides
`SKILL.md` that the bundle excludes and the `.gitignore` of the work tree allow, with a description taken from the
frontmatter of each Markdown file. Same machine and method as above.

| Bundle | ms/op | B/op | allocs/op |
| ------ | ----- | ---- | --------- |
| One skill, 1 file | 2.9 | 428 KB | 1466 |
| One skill, 100 files | 5.7 | 1.7 MB | 9303 |
| One skill, 2000 files | 52.3 | 26.1 MB | 157556 |
| 200 skills of 10 files each | 839 | 119 MB | 538587 |

A bundle has a fixed cost of about 3 ms (the two git processes that ask which files .gitignore leaves out, one since
the fifth pass) and then 25 us per file. The 2000-file bundle is
at the file limit of an installed skill.

The external scanner stage (`ScannerStage`) is what a `[[lint.external]]` scanner needs before it starts anything:
listing the staged files, digesting them and computing the cache key. The key itself is 4-5 us whatever the size.

| Skills (4 files each) | Stage listing | Digest | Cache key |
| --------------------- | ------------- | ------ | --------- |
| 50 | 1.45 ms, 612 KB, 3821 allocs | 0.25 ms, 17 KB | 5.0 us |
| 500 | 14.4 ms, 6.2 MB, 38043 allocs | 2.69 ms, 164 KB | 4.1 us |

Both grow linearly. A scanner run on a warm cache therefore costs the stage listing plus the digest, 1.7 ms for 50
skills and 17 ms for 500.

`generate` end to end on the 200-file benchmark project (`GeneratePresets`, median of 3), with 2, 10 and all 55
built-in presets:

| Presets | Full generate | B/op | No-op generate | B/op |
| ------- | ------------- | ---- | -------------- | ---- |
| 2 | 243 ms | 19.9 MB | 142 ms | 26.6 MB |
| 10 | 500 ms | 61.6 MB | 213 ms | 73.0 MB |
| 55 | 1882 ms | 269 MB | 670 ms | 309 MB |

The time is spent writing the outputs (a temporary file and a rename per output) and rendering, about 30 ms per
preset; nothing in it was changed.

#### Optimization passes

Numbers are time/op and B/op on an Apple M5 Pro that was running other builds at the same time (load average near
50), taken as alternating runs of test binaries built from the commits below, so the ratios are reliable and the
absolute values are not. Behavior is unchanged: the golden tests and every existing test pass, and each change that
could alter a result has a test comparing it with the code it replaced.

| Path (benchmark) | Change | Before | After |
| ---------------- | ------ | ------ | ----- |
| Credential scan of clean text, 37 KB (`lint SecretScan/DetectSecret/clean/large`) | each credential pattern runs only on text holding one of its literals | 6.1 ms | 0.30 ms (20x) |
| Credential redaction of clean text (`SecretScan/RedactSecrets/clean/large`) | same gate in `secretpat.Redact` and `lint.RedactSecrets` | 6.1 ms, 0.9 MB | 0.28 ms, 0 B |
| Redaction of text holding secrets (`SecretScan/RedactSecrets/dirty/large`) | same gate | 6.1 ms, 0.9 MB | 2.5 ms, 0.33 MB |
| Security scan of one text (`SecretScan/ScanText/clean/large`) | credential gate, then literal gates on the shell-exec (`curl`, `wget`, `base64`, `eval`, `chmod`, `>`) and instruction-override patterns | 29 ms | 7.6 ms (3.8x) |
| Same scan, allocations | ASCII-only lines skip the rune conversion and seen-set of the hidden-character scan | 1.33 MB | 1.18 MB (-11%) |
| Configured secret patterns, 400 lines x 2 patterns (`SecretScanCustomPatterns`) | compiled once per run, not once per scanned line | 12 ms, 7.7 MB | 8 ms, 1.1 MB |
| Lint of 200 content files (`lint RunFull/medium`) | all of the above, tree-relative paths memoized per run, backtick-token prose check only for path-like tokens | 570-660 ms, 53.5 MB, 667k allocs | 265-335 ms, 47.1 MB, 617k allocs |
| Frontmatter parse of a 570 KB document (`parser ParseFrontmatter/longbody`) | find the closing marker by scanning instead of splitting and re-joining the document | 83.6 us, 228 KB | 10.2 us, 7 KB (8x) |
| Frontmatter parse of 200 documents (`ParseFrontmatterBatch/medium`) | same | 1.29 ms, 2.09 MB | 1.0 ms, 1.59 MB |
| Any-file verifier regex, 1000-file tree (`verifiers RegexFiles/medium`) | exclude globs compiled once per predicate, not once per matching file | 13.2 ms, 19.8 MB, 174k allocs | 1.3 ms, 61 KB, 238 allocs (10x) |

The shell and instruction-override pre-checks compare ASCII literals without case in place and treat U+017F and
U+212A as the `s` and `k` the patterns' case folding makes them, so a line the pattern would match always reaches it.

##### Second pass: repeated loads, publish at scale, startup

Same method as above, taken on a quieter machine (load average near 20): test binaries built from the commit before
the pass and from the last commit of it, run back to back with `-benchtime=3x -count=2` (`1x` for the 2000-file
project), so the ratios are reliable and the absolute values are not. Output is unchanged: `tests/golden` passes
without edits.

| Path (benchmark) | Change | Before | After |
| ---------------- | ------ | ------ | ----- |
| `lock --check`, 200 files (`commands Lock/check/medium`) | the configuration is loaded once and shared by the content comparison, the tag check and the signature check (it was loaded three times); one repository-question memo per check | 1.5 s, 71.4 MB, 274k allocs, 16 git processes | 0.45 s, 45.1 MB, 192k allocs, 10 git processes |
| `lock --check`, 10 files (`Lock/check/small`) | same | 29 ms, 2.19 MB | 9.6 ms, 1.36 MB |
| `lock --check`, 2000 files (`Lock/check/large`) | same | 596 MB, 2.24M allocs | 393 MB, 1.69M allocs |
| `publish --dry-run`, 10 files (`PublishDryRun/bundle/small`) | the load is shared by the lock check, trap files are read at their size instead of into a 1 MiB buffer, the source hash is streamed into the digest, and one memo serves the whole run | 1.49 s, 49.6 MB, 27 git processes | 0.66 s, 37.7 MB, 22 git processes |
| `publish --dry-run`, 200 files (`PublishDryRun/bundle/medium`) | same | 4.3 s, 280 MB, 770k allocs | 2.2 s, 152 MB, 656k allocs |
| `publish --dry-run`, 2000 files (`PublishDryRun/bundle/large`) | same | 2.51 GB, 10.5M allocs | 1.36 GB, 9.89M allocs (-46% bytes) |
| Numbered-path reference check (`lint NumberedPrefixExists`, 100 lookups over 20,000 paths) | the paths are sorted once per tree and each lookup is a binary search, instead of listing and scanning every path per numeric token | 181 ms, 33.2 MB | 0.04 ms, 4.9 KB |
| Generator secret gate (`generator SecretGate/small`, `medium`) | `generate` runs it under a context that remembers `git rev-parse` answers, so the gate asks git once, not twice | 3.5 MB, 13.4k allocs; 3.7 MB, 15.0k allocs; 2 git processes | 1.9 MB, 7.4k allocs; 2.1 MB, 8.6k allocs; 1 git process |
| Process start (`ai-rulez --version`, `GODEBUG=inittrace=1`) | package-level regular expressions of `lint`, `evalimport`, `cmd/commands` and `secretpat` compile on first use (`sync.OnceValue`) instead of at start | 11.7 MB allocated by package init (6.8 MB in ai-rulez packages) | 9.1 MB (4.2 MB) |

What changed where:

- `lock --check` and `publish --dry-run` load once and thread the result. The memo (`gitutil.WithMemo`) is attached to
  the context of one `generate`, `drift`, `lock --check` or `publish` run and dies with it; it is never process-wide,
  and the long-lived callers (the MCP server, the doctor, watch mode) do not get one. Questions about history
  (`HEAD`, refs, file lists) are not memoized.
- The 2.5 GB of `publish --dry-run` at 2000 files was mostly one allocation: the trap check read every candidate
  file into a fresh 1 MiB buffer. The source hash text (built whole, hashed, dropped) and the repeated configuration
  loads of the lock check were the next removable allocations.
- Package-level regular expressions in the four packages are lazy. The `global` archlint rule treats a
  `sync.OnceValue` the way it treats `regexp.MustCompile` (immutable in practice); the three existing
  `OnceValue` globals (in `ard`, `tokens` and `generator/settings`) lose one allowlisted site each.

Behavior that changed deliberately (everything else is byte-identical):

- Frontmatter is split by `internal/frontmatter` in the config loader (`parseFrontmatter`,
  `hasUnclosedFrontmatter`, `FrontmatterProblem`, `IsOKFListing`), in lint (`parseDoc`) and in the generator
  (`frontmatterEnd`, hash injection, `listingFrontmatter`, `ruleFileFrontmatter`, `mappedFrontmatterFields`). Its
  rules now apply to all of them: a UTF-8 BOM before the opening fence is ignored (the loader and the generator used
  to treat the file as having no frontmatter); a fence may carry trailing spaces or tabs, and an indented `---`
  is not a fence (the loader and lint used to trim both sides); the empty block `---`/`---` is a block (the loader
  needed three lines); the blank line after a CRLF block is dropped from the body as it is after an LF block;
  `ruleFileFrontmatter` no longer skips blank lines before the opening fence and no longer takes `---foo` for a
  closing fence; hash injection into a block closed on its first line works. `internal/frontmatter.ClosingLine`
  finds the closing line without building the block, so lint does not copy the YAML.
- Readers now refuse input over their limit through `safefs.ReadLimited` instead of passing a cut one on: an
  attestation file over `MaxBundleBytes` (AR721 at the read, not at the parse), the GitHub token and Sigstore
  service responses over their caps, and the publish inputs (templates, the lock, skill files, dist files and
  tar entries), the signing key, the LLM cache entry and secret. `safefs.ReadFileLimited` opens and reads with the same
  bound.

##### Third pass: the process cleanup after each spawn

`internal/runner` ends every run by killing what the command left behind. The guarantee, from the code and the
tests (`TestRunKillsHelpersThatLeaveTheGroup`, `TestRunKillsADetachedSystemBinary`, `TestConcurrentRunsDoNotKillEachOther`):
after `Run` returns, no process of the run is alive. That covers the process group, any descendant seen while the
command ran (a helper that called `setsid` or `setpgid` is still a descendant), and a helper that detached and was
reparented to init between two looks at the table, which is found by the run token every child inherits in its
environment or by the write end of the marker pipe every child inherits as a descriptor (macOS withholds the
environment of platform binaries, so there the descriptor is what finds them). It does not cover a helper that drops
both the variable and the descriptor before detaching, and it must never touch a process of another run. On Windows
the job object gives the guarantee without any table read.

The cost was in the token and descriptor search (`adoptCarriers`): it skips processes older than the command's root
(a descendant cannot be older than its ancestor), but a `Spec.ShortLived` run (every git call) does not read the
process table at start, so it never learned the root's start time and the search covered every process of the user,
one `sysctl` (macOS) or `/proc/<pid>/environ` read (Linux) each, after every spawn.

Now a short-lived run reads the start time of its own root with a single lookup at attach (`processStart`: one
`sysctl kern.proc.pid`, or one `/proc/<pid>/stat`), so the search covers only processes that started since the command,
which is a handful. If that lookup fails the search is unbounded as before, so the guarantee is the same on every
platform; nothing was weakened. The full (non-short) path already had the bound and is unchanged. Windows is unchanged.

Measured on a loaded machine (load average 16 to 28, 850 processes), `go test -bench` of the runner and generator
packages, test binaries built before and after and run back to back. Wall times are dominated by the fork cost under
that load and are not reliable; the allocations and the isolated sweep are.

| Path (benchmark) | Before | After |
| ---------------- | ------ | ----- |
| Sweep alone over the real table of 850 processes (`runner AdoptCarriers`) | 9.5 ms, 1.5 MB, 10k allocs | 0.02 to 0.04 ms, 544 B, 9 allocs |
| One short-lived spawn with cleanup (`runner SpawnCleanup/short`) | 1.85 MB, 7.3k to 7.8k allocs | 0.78 MB, 300 to 420 allocs |
| One full spawn with cleanup (`SpawnCleanup/full`) | unchanged | unchanged |
| Secret gate, 10 files (`generator SecretGate/small`) | 4.2 to 4.5 MB, 18k to 19k allocs | 2.1 MB, 3.7k allocs |
| Secret gate with the memo (`SecretGate/small-memo`) | 2.4 to 2.5 MB, 10k to 11k allocs | 0.9 to 1.2 MB, 0.8k to 2.4k allocs |

The cost of the sweep now depends on how many processes start during the command, not on how many exist.

##### Fourth pass: CPU of `generate` and `validate`

v5.0.0 spent about four times the CPU of 4.23 in `generate` (and more in `validate`). A CPU profile (a temporary
`pprof` hook, not committed) put about half of `generate` in the authored-content secret gate, which called
`lint.RunWith` with `SecurityOnly` although it reads only AR001: every file went through the shell, injection,
hidden-character, host and blob scans, and the markdown file was split into lines twice (`newScanText`, dominated by
backtracking in `negRe`). `validate` paid the same duplicate splits plus unconditional regular expressions in the body
scan.

Measured on a 590-file, 2.6 MB project, user+sys CPU of the whole command, alternating runs of binaries built before
and after (load average high; sys time is file I/O and did not change):

| Command | user before | user after | user+sys before | user+sys after |
| ------- | ----------- | ---------- | --------------- | -------------- |
| `generate` | 1.40 s | 0.65 s | 3.3 to 3.6 s | 2.3 to 2.4 s |
| `validate` | 1.9 s | 1.6 s | 3.6 s | 3.2 to 3.3 s |
| `tokens` | 0.69 s | 0.69 s | 1.9 s | 1.9 s (unchanged) |

Secret gate alone (`lint AuthoredSecretGate/medium`, 200 files): 106 to 161 ms, 13.0 MB, 115.6k allocs with the full
security family; 33 ms, 2.9 MB, 20.4k allocs with `Options.SecretsOnly` (3 to 5x).

- `Options.SecretsOnly` (with `SecurityOnly`) runs only the units that reach `securityScan` (item scan, resources,
  imported content) and checks each line against the credential patterns alone. Inline ignores, severities,
  `ignore`, `example_paths`, configured patterns and the imported-content level go through the same `add`, so the AR001
  findings are identical (`TestSecretsOnlyMatchesSecurityOnly`).
- `scanTextOf` memoizes the split text per file and content for the run (security scan, text scans, capability
  profile); a `scanText` is never modified after it is built (`TestScanTextOfMemoizesPerFileAndText`).
- The body scan skips link, backtick and name patterns on lines lacking a literal every match contains
  (`TestBodyScanGatesAgreeWithThePatterns` compares gated and ungated results). `generate` output and
  `validate`/`validate --strict`/`tokens` output on the benchmark project are byte-identical to the previous binary.

`tokens` is dominated by cl100k counting and file reads, and was not changed (the token memo is the separate branch
named below). What remains of `generate` is file I/O (loading, output safety checks, writes).

##### Fifth pass: the security scan and the git questions

Test binaries built from the commit before the pass and from its last commit, run alternately three times on the
machine described under Monorepo index; medians. The `Benchmarks` job of CI failed on main because
`SecretScan/ScanText` was 72-93% over `scripts/bench-baseline.txt` (the 25% gate): the rules
`credential-store-instruction` and `permission-bypass-instruction` had been added since the baseline and ran their
regular expressions on every prose line. They now run behind literal checks, like the other text scans.

| Path (benchmark) | Change | Before | After |
| ---------------- | ------ | ------ | ----- |
| Security scan of one text, 37 KB (`lint SecretScan/ScanText/clean/large`) | credential-store scan runs its regular expressions only on a line holding a store path or a word a store is named by; each permission-bypass pattern runs only on a line holding its rarest word (not "auto", which "author" holds); the case-folded stem search jumps between candidate letters | 20.1 ms | 10.9 ms (-46%) |
| Same, 3 KB (`ScanText/clean/small`) | same | 1.20 ms | 0.66 ms (-45%) |
| Same, text with secrets (`ScanText/dirty/large`) | same | 20.1 ms | 10.7 ms (-47%) |
| Security analyzer of a 200-file project (`lint Analyzers/security`) | same | 74.3 ms | 42.7 ms (-43%) |
| Lint of 200 content files (`RunFull/medium`) | same | 146 ms | 112 ms (-24%) |
| Catalog build with discovery, 20000 files, 10 / 100 / 500 scopes (`mcp DiscoveryCatalog`) | same (the scan of every served item) | 82 / 441 / 2246 ms | 62 / 306 / 1239 ms (-24% / -31% / -45%) |
| One installed skill of 1 file (`config LoadSkillResourcesContext/files=1`) | the bundle filter skips `git ls-files` when `git check-ignore` already says the directory is no work tree (two processes became one) | 5.9 ms, 828 KB, 2690 allocs | 2.9 ms, 428 KB, 1466 allocs (-51%) |
| 200 installed skills of 10 files (`LoadSkillResourcesCatalog`) | same | 1386 ms, 199 MB | 839 ms, 119 MB (-39%) |

Output is unchanged: `TestMayNameCredentialKeepsEveryStore`, `TestBypassStemsKeepEveryPattern` and
`TestIndexFoldASCIIAgreesWithTheReference` compare each gate with the pattern it guards, and the existing lint
tests pass. Two benchmarks also failed outright and were fixed: `BenchmarkProjectTools` called tools with a
`working_directory` outside the server's confinement, and `BenchmarkSkillServer/load_skill` hit the 256 KiB session
budget once `N` passed about 2700. CI did not report it, because `task test:benchmark | tee` returned tee's exit status;
the step now runs with `pipefail`. `scripts/bench-baseline.txt` still holds numbers from before the new rules and
should be re-recorded from the CI artifact (`bench-subset.txt`).

Measured and left alone: the 10.9 ms that remains in `ScanText/clean/large` is spread over about thirty rules, none
above 10%; the index build proper (listing, classification, reads) is under 10% of a catalog build, so its per-item cost (20-35 us, mostly the YAML parse and
the read) was not worth changing.

#### What dominates elsewhere

These were measured and not changed here.

- **Process spawns per content file.** Loading a project with 200 skills took 91 s on the loaded machine before the
  branch that batches `git ls-files` and `git check-ignore` per directory (0.5 s with it). The remaining
  wall time of `generate`, `clean`, `lock` and `publish` on 200 to 2000 files is mostly git (`rev-parse`,
  `ls-files`) and file-system calls; their CPU time is a small share.
- **Token counting.** cl100k counting of the prompt text is the largest allocator in a lint run (about a third of
  the bytes, in `regexp2` match objects); the memo that removes it is part of the same separate branch.
- **Served skills.** `lock --check` still builds the served-skill views twice (`mcp.DynamicLockChanges` loads the
  configuration for each view and scans the skills); that code lives in `internal/mcp`.
- **Publish at scale.** What remains of `publish --dry-run` at 2000 files (1.36 GB over 9.9 million objects) is the
  strict lint run (about 60%, mostly cl100k token counting in `regexp2`, which the separate token memo branch
  removes), the lock comparison and the served views.

## Architecture

Source: https://goldziher.github.io/ai-rulez/architecture/

How ai-rulez turns a source tree into the native files of 52 harnesses, and where each step lives in the code. Read this
before changing the load, render or lint paths; for what each option does, see [Configuration](configuration.md).

#### The pipeline

Every command that reads a project goes through the same stages:

```text
load  ->  merge  ->  validate  ->  render  ->  write
```

| Stage | What happens | Code |
| ----- | ------------ | ---- |
| **Load** | Find the configuration (`.ai-rulez/config.toml`, `.config/ai-rulez/config.toml` or `.agents/ai-rulez.toml`), read it through a `workspace` view, scan the content tree and fetch what it references. | `internal/project`, `internal/config`, `internal/workspace` |
| **Merge** | Layer `config.<name>.toml` files (`default_layers`, `AI_RULEZ_LAYERS`) and the machine-local `config.local.toml` over the base file, fold in the `plugins/` and `marketplaces/` definition files, resolve includes, installed skills and builtin packs. | `internal/config`, `internal/includes`, `internal/skillsource`, `internal/builtins` |
| **Validate** | Reject an invalid configuration (unknown or conflicting keys, a profile that names nothing, `[plugin]` combined with `[[plugins_authoring]]`) and enforce the [organization policy](policy.md) before anything is rendered; `validate` adds the content checks. | `Config.Validate`, `internal/policy`, `internal/lint` |
| **Render** | Resolve the profile (or `--role`), collect MCP servers and render every preset into a plan: the files to write, merge into or remove, each with a digest. Nothing is written yet. | `internal/generator` |
| **Write** | Apply the plan: write outputs, merge settings documents, remove stale files, update the manifest, lock and the managed `.gitignore` block. | `internal/generator` (appliers) |

`internal/config` cannot import the packages that implement includes, installed skills, the `.agents` source or the
presets, and they import it, so `internal/project` joins them into one set of resolvers. The CLI, the MCP server and the
public API in `pkg/airulez` all load a project through it.

##### Plan and apply

`generate` is `Plan` followed by `Apply` with an applier. The plan is the same whichever applier runs it, which is why the
modes cannot disagree about what a run would do:

| Applier | Used by | Effect |
| ------- | ------- | ------ |
| disk | `generate` | writes the plan |
| dry run | `generate --dry-run` | lists what the disk applier would do |
| check | `generate --check` | compares the plan with the disk and the managed `.gitignore` block, writes nothing, exits 2 on drift |
| describe | `generate --emit-plan`, `pkg/airulez` | reports the plan as a JSON document ([schema](https://github.com/Goldziher/ai-rulez/blob/main/schema/plan.schema.json)) |

Two presets that write the same path must render identical bytes, or the plan fails and names both. Settings files such as
`.claude/settings.json`, `opencode.json` and `.codex/config.toml` are merged document by document: ai-rulez owns the keys
it writes and keeps the rest, comments included.

##### Presets

The 52 harness presets are the entries the registry returns as individual presets. 42 are declarative provider specs
(`internal/generator/providers/builtin/*.toml`, plus the `mcp` spec), ten are Go presets in
`internal/generator/presets` (`antigravity`, `baz`, `cline`, `codex`, `copilot`, `cursor`, `devin`, `gemini`, `opencode`,
`xum`). `okf` and `llms-txt` are output presets that are not harnesses and are not counted. `tests/golden` records the
output of every preset, so a new preset cannot land without a golden. See [Supported harnesses](harnesses.md).

#### Three source layouts

The same pipeline reads three layouts. They differ only in the load stage; everything after it works on the same content
tree.

| Layout | Selected by | Content lives in | Written by `generate` |
| ------ | ----------- | ---------------- | --------------------- |
| `.ai-rulez` | the default | `.ai-rulez/` (`rules/`, `context/`, `skills/`, `agents/`, `commands/`, `checks/`, `domains/`) | every preset's files, including `AGENTS.md` |
| `.agents` and `AGENTS.md` | `source = "agents"`, or a configuration in `.agents/ai-rulez.toml` | the root and nested `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/` | every preset's files **except** `AGENTS.md` and anything under `.agents/` |
| OKF | an `index.md` bundle; the `okf` preset | an [OKF](okf.md) bundle, which is also what `.ai-rulez/` is internally | the bundle, with `export okf` |

**`.ai-rulez` as OKF.** `.ai-rulez/` is an OKF bundle: `init`, `add` and the MCP tools write concepts with `type`, `title`
and `x-ai-rulez` frontmatter and refresh the `index.md` files. `internal/okfbridge` maps content to and from a bundle,
`internal/okf` reads and validates bundles. A tree without a root `index.md` is the legacy layout and still loads with a
deprecation notice.

**`.agents` and `AGENTS.md`.** `internal/agentssource` completes what the content scan found under `.agents`: it adds the
root `AGENTS.md` as the context item `agents` (or one item per `##` heading with `agents_md_split = true`), reads every
nested `AGENTS.md` as context scoped to its directory (`agents-<dir>`, glob `<dir>/**`), and drops files that carry the
generated header, so a project that switched source is not fed its own output. The nested walk honours `.gitignore` inside a
git repository, skips symlinks and dependency trees, and stops at a directory that is a project of its own. On the way out,
the generator drops every output that would land on `AGENTS.md` or under `.agents/` (also through a symlink), so `generate`
and `generate --check` leave the standard's files alone. `generate --watch` watches `AGENTS.md`, `.agents` and the nested
files found at each run. Details: [.agents as a source](agents-source.md).

**OKF.** `export okf` and `import okf` convert between a bundle and the content tree; `okf validate <dir>` lints any bundle
with the `AR9B` codes without a configuration. See [OKF](okf.md).

#### Recursive runs

`generate --recursive`, `generate --check --recursive` and `validate --recursive` find every configuration root below the
working directory and process them concurrently on at most one worker per CPU (`GOMAXPROCS`; `validate --external` uses
one). Two properties keep the result deterministic:

- **Ordered output.** For `generate --check --recursive` and `validate --recursive` the roots finish in any order but are
  emitted in path order, each as a `[n/N] path (elapsed)` line on stderr. A slow first root delays the print, never
  reorders it, and the exit code does not depend on timing. `--quiet` and a structured `--format` silence the lines.
- **Per-root warnings.** Each root collects the log records its work raises (`internal/diag`, `rootNotes` in
  `cmd/commands`) and the run prints them with that root's result. The writing `generate --recursive` shows a progress
  counter and logs a root's load warnings as they happen.

A recursive run with `gitignore = true` writes one managed block per git repository, at that repository's toplevel,
holding the patterns of the roots inside it, and `--check` verifies each block once after the last root. A root's
patterns never reach the `.gitignore` of another repository or of a root with `gitignore = false`. See
[Monorepo](monorepo.md).

#### The managed `.gitignore` block

With `gitignore = true` (or `generate --gitignore`) ai-rulez maintains a `# BEGIN ai-rulez` / `# END ai-rulez` block in
`.gitignore`, and edits nothing outside it. The default is off, because generated files are meant to be committed.

- The entries are the specific generated files and owned subtrees, never an assistant directory as a whole.
- Before writing, the generator asks git (`git check-ignore`) about each entry against every ignore source with its own
  block left out. An entry already ignored by your rules, or re-included by a negation of yours, is left out of the block.
- `gitignore_exclude` lists generated outputs you commit on purpose; they stay out of the block while every other entry stays
  managed. Machine-local and secret outputs are never excluded.
- The block is the same on every machine and with or without `--no-local`. It always lists `.ai-rulez/config.local.*`
  (and the overlay's `.config.local.*` lock and temp files), `.ai-rulez/local/` and the machine-local manifest, whether
  or not those exist. It never lists a path only because this machine's local inputs add it: outputs the overlay or
  `local/` content creates (`CLAUDE.local.md`, a hook-only `.claude/settings.json`, local skills) are kept in
  `.git/info/exclude`, which is not committed.
- With `gitignore = false` the machine-local inputs that exist (`config.local.*`, `local/`) are still ignored, and an
  MCP config holding secrets is refused unless git ignores it. A machine-local manifest that is the only local file goes
  to `.git/info/exclude`, so `generate` does not write a tracked `.gitignore` for a project that turned it off.
- `generate --check` reports a block that differs from what a run would write as drift, and `generate` warns when a tracked
  file matches a line of the block.

Code: `internal/gitignore` (the fenced block), `internal/generator/gitignore*.go` (patterns, probes, the recursive sink).

#### Plugins, marketplaces and Agent Plugins

`generate --plugin` is a second render over the same content tree. It builds distributable bundles instead of project
files:

1. **Definitions.** `[plugin]` bundles the whole root. Several plugins come from `[[plugins_authoring]]` entries (or
   `[[marketplace.plugins]]`), each selecting skills, commands, agents, domains, MCP servers and hooks by name or glob; an
   empty selector bundles nothing. `[[marketplaces_authoring]]` entries each list plugin definitions by name. Each definition
   can live in `plugins/<name>.toml` or `marketplaces/<name>.toml`, and a layer can add, override or remove one by `name`.
   `[plugin]` and `[[plugins_authoring]]` cannot be combined, nor `[marketplace]` and `[[marketplaces_authoring]]`.
2. **Bundles.** For each plugin and each runtime (`claude`, `codex`, `cursor`, `gemini`, `kimi`, `opencode`, `factory`,
   `hermes`, and the opt-in `pi`, `copilot` and `agent-plugins`) `internal/generator/plugin` writes the runtime's manifest and
   content under `<output_dir>/plugins/<name>/`, with provenance headers.
3. **Marketplace indexes.** One index per marketplace (`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`, plus the Codex and Cursor indexes
   where a listed plugin targets them), each directory publishable on its own and each with a provenance sidecar.
4. **Verify.** `verify --plugin` regenerates in memory and reports drift per plugin and marketplace.
5. **Publish.** `publish` runs `validate --strict`, `lock --check`, `verify --plugin` and a secret scan, then writes a
   byte-reproducible archive, manifest, `SHA256SUMS`, the lock and release notes; `--to` with `--execute --yes` pushes to a
   GitHub release, npm or an OCI registry. Emitters turn the published plugin into other formats: `agent-plugins`
   ([Agent Plugins](agent-plugins.md), `internal/agentplugins`), `ard` ([ARD](ard.md), `internal/ard`) and `mcp-server-card`
   ([MCP server cards](mcp-server-card.md), `internal/mcpcard`), plus the Cursor team marketplace and experimental ones.
   Emitters are pure functions of the manifest: no network, clock or file system.

`internal/agentplugins` and `internal/ard` do not import the config loader; callers map their content to a model, which is
what makes their output deterministic and testable against the vendored schemas in `tests/conformance`. See
[Authoring plugins](plugins.md) and [Publish](publish.md).

#### The lint pipeline

`validate` and `scan` run on the same engine (`internal/lint`); `scan` selects only the security analyzers.

```text
configuration or implicit root  ->  targets  ->  analyzers  ->  filters  ->  report  ->  exit code
```

1. **Configuration or implicit root.** With a configuration, the content tree is the subject. Without one, `validate`, `scan`
   and `doctor` use an *implicit* configuration: no presets, hooks or MCP servers, default `[lint]` settings, the repository
   toplevel as the root. The content is found by convention (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md`, `SKILL.md`, `.claude/`,
   `.agents/`, `.cursor/rules`, plugin manifests, hook files, `.mcp.json`) and treated as hand-written. A line on stderr
   says so; nothing is written. `generate`, `clean` and `lock` still need a configuration.
2. **Targets.** `--path`, `--glob` and `[lint] paths` add files outside the content tree, such as a marketplace in a
   directory of its own; with an implicit root they replace the detection. Every target must resolve inside the repository
   root. A file is classified by its content (a plugin manifest, a marketplace, a hook file, an MCP file) or by its name and
   place (`SKILL.md`, `AGENTS.md`), and a file that cannot be linted is named, not dropped. A text file of no known kind gets
   the secret scan only.
3. **Outputs.** `--outputs` (or `[lint] lint_outputs`) also lints the generated files: the bytes `generate` writes or would
   write, plus the files its last run recorded. Only the analyzers that judge what a model reads (security, references,
   descriptions) run over them, a finding is marked as output, and a problem the authored source already has is reported once.
4. **Analyzers.** `security`, `references`, `hooks`, `mcp`, `duplicates`, `descriptions`, `budgets`, `metadata`, `plugin`,
   `config`, `roles`, `lock`, `delivery`, `evals`, `okf`, `llmstxt`, `traps`, `convert`, `search` and `verifiers`;
   `--analyzer` runs a chosen subset. Each finding has a stable `AR` code, a severity and a `file:line`.
5. **Filters.** `[lint.severity]` and `[lint.ignore]`, the baseline, and `--since` / `--changed` (with the reference hops that
   pull in dependent files).
6. **Report and exit code.** Text, JSON, SARIF, GitHub annotations, JUnit or Markdown. `0` valid, `1` the configuration is
   invalid or a named target could not be read, `2` findings at or above `--fail-on`.

`--recursive` repeats this per root and merges the findings. See [Strict validation](strict-validation.md).

#### Judge

`ai-rulez judge` is the one lint-adjacent command that calls a model. It runs in any repository: the models come from flags,
`AI_RULEZ_LLM_*` variables and the user config, never from the repository, and the key from the provider's own variable.

`cmd/commands/judge*.go` discovers the units (a skill directory, or one file: agents, commands, rules, `CLAUDE.md`,
`AGENTS.md`, MCP and settings files, `.claude/` at any depth), runs the `validate` analyzers over them for static facts, and
reads the `[judge]` table. `internal/judge` is the engine and does no I/O of its own: it attaches the rules and `CLAUDE.md`
files that apply to each unit, builds the nonce-fenced prompts, plans the calls under the caps, verifies every quote against
the text that was sent, asks the adjudicator, and computes scores, statuses and the decision in code. `internal/llm` is the
single abstraction that calls the model (and resolves and refreshes AWS credentials for Bedrock). Nothing is sent without
`--allow-llm`, `--estimate` shows the units, the egress host, the models and the cost estimate and sends nothing, and
`--max-cost` caps the spend. `bench/judge` is its evaluation. See [Judge](judge.md); for scored review with calibration, see
[Review](review.md).

`targetmatch` and `userscope` (the user-level layout of each harness).

`pkg/airulez` is the public Go API over the same engine: load a project from a directory, memory or a commit, validate it, plan
or apply a generate run, and write or check the lock. `tests/archlint` keeps ambient authority out of `internal/`.

## Standards Conformance

Source: https://goldziher.github.io/ai-rulez/standards/

ai-rulez claims conformance with a standard only when a passing test backs the claim. Every test named here is in
[`tests/conformance`](https://github.com/Goldziher/ai-rulez/tree/main/tests/conformance) and runs with `go test ./...`. It
validates a golden or freshly generated document against the standard's own schema, vendored and pinned under
`tests/conformance/schemas`, with no network access. The README in that directory says how to refresh a schema.

Status values:

- **conformant**: our output validates against the standard's official machine-readable schema in a test.
- **partial**: tested, but the standard has no official schema (the test transcribes its written rules), or only part of
  what we emit is covered. The gaps column says what is missing.

| Standard | Pinned version | Status | What we generate and validate | Test | Known gaps |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Agent Plugins](https://agent-plugins.org) | 1.0.0 (published, default) and 1.1.0 (working draft); [schema repo](https://github.com/agentplugins/agent-plugins-spec) at `ff8ab5e` | conformant | `plugin.json`, `mcp.json` and `skills/` from `generate --plugin`; read back and checked by `validate` ([page](agent-plugins.md)) | `TestAgentPluginsGoldenConformsToTheOfficialSchemas`, `TestAgentPluginsGeneratedByTheCLIConformToTheOfficialSchemas` | The official name pattern uses a lookahead RE2 cannot compile; the test applies the same rule in Go. Extension namespaces are not schema-checked beyond the base manifest. |
| [ARD](https://agenticresourcediscovery.org/) | 0.91 (proposal); [ard-spec](https://github.com/ards-project/ard-spec) at `b76f235` | conformant | `ard.json` from `publish --emit ard`; entry and manifest schema plus the URN grammar ([page](ard.md)) | `TestARDManifestGoldenConformsToTheEntrySchema`, `TestARDValidatorAcceptsTheGoldenAndNamesItsSpecVersion` | The spec is a proposal; media types and term names can change. The plugin entry type is an ai-rulez vendor type. The golden comes from the in-package model, not a release. |
| [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org/) | No versioned release; format as published at llmstxt.org | partial | `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` from the `llms-txt` preset, and for the docs site ([page](llms-txt.md)) | `TestGeneratedLLMSTxtFollowsTheFormat`, `TestPublishedDocsSiteLLMSTxtFollowsTheFormat` | No official schema. The test transcribes the format (H1, optional blockquote, H2 link lists). `llms-full.txt` is checked for its H1 only; the format does not define it. |
| [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/specification) | No versioned release; specification as published at agentskills.io | partial | `SKILL.md` for every skill, with its resources, under `.claude/skills`, `.agents/skills` and `skills/` ([page](skills.md)) | `TestGeneratedSkillsFollowTheAgentSkillsSpecification`, plus the skill checks in the Agent Plugins tests | No official schema. The test transcribes the frontmatter rules (name, description, compatibility, license, metadata, allowed-tools). Resource layout is not checked. |
| [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md) | No versioned release | partial | `AGENTS.md` at the project root ([page](agents-md.md)) | `TestGeneratedAgentsMDIsPlainMarkdownAtTheRoot` | The format has no schema and no required fields. The test checks that the file is plain Markdown at the root with the project's guidance. Nested `AGENTS.md` files in monorepos are not covered. |
| MCP server configuration | The `mcp.json` schema of Agent Plugins 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 | partial | `mcp.json` (stdio, streamable-http and sse servers) | `TestMCPServerEntriesUseTheSchemaTransportTypes`, plus the `mcp.json` schema check in the Agent Plugins tests | The per-harness files (`.mcp.json`, `.codex/config.toml` and others) follow each tool's own format and are not validated against a schema here. |
| [MCP server card](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/seps/2127-mcp-server-cards) | SEP-2127 (Final); the schema is `schema.json` of the experimental [server-card extension](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/experimental-ext-server-card) (Apache-2.0) at `526201b` | partial (experimental extension, pinned `526201b`) | One `<server>.json` per remote `[[mcp_servers]]` entry from `publish --emit mcp-server-card`, and the same card embedded as `application/mcp-server-card+json` entries in `ard.json` ([page](mcp-server-card.md)) | `TestMCPServerCardGoldensConformToTheExtensionSchema`, `TestMCPServerCardBuilderOutputConformsToTheExtensionSchema`, `TestMCPServerCardSchemaRejectsWhatACardMustNotBe` | The schema is generated from `schema.ts` by an experimental extension, not yet a published versioned schema; it can change. A card describes remote servers only, so stdio servers get none. Identity beyond name, version and description (title, icons, repository, website), URL variables and `_meta` are not generated. `validate` does not check cards; only the conformance tests do. |
| [CycloneDX](https://cyclonedx.org/) | 1.6 | conformant | `ai-rulez sbom` ([page](sbom.md)) | `TestCycloneDXOutputConformsToTheOfficial16Schema` | The test validates structure. NTIA minimum-element and license-expression policy checks are not run. |
| [SPDX](https://spdx.dev/) | 2.3 (JSON) | conformant | `ai-rulez sbom --type spdx-json` | `TestSPDXOutputConformsToTheOfficial23Schema` | Structure only. The in-package tests also check unique identifiers and resolving relationships. |
| [in-toto Statement](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation) and [DSSE](https://github.com/secure-systems-lab/dsse) | Statement v1; DSSE v1 | partial | Signed statements inside Sigstore bundles from `ai-rulez sign`; `verify` checks them ([page](signing.md)) | `TestSignedStatementIsADSSEEnvelopeOverAnInTotoStatement` | Neither project publishes a JSON Schema, so the vendored schemas are hand-written from the specifications. Sigstore bundle structure and certificate chains are covered by `internal/signing` tests, not by a conformance schema. The `v0.1` statement type is accepted on verification only. |
| OKF | v0.2 | not covered here | Native format ([page](okf.md)) | `internal/okf` | Tracked in [#281](https://github.com/Goldziher/ai-rulez/issues/281). |
| OpenTelemetry (OTLP) | n/a | not covered here | Export only ([page](telemetry.md)) | n/a | No document we write is validated against an OTLP schema. |

#### Standards first, extensions second

Future ai-rulez versions will always follow the AGENTS.md and Agent Skills standards. With `source = "agents"` the
root `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` are read as those standards define them. The folders ai-rulez
adds beside them (`.agents/rules`, `agents`, `checks`, `commands`, `context` and `domains`) are extensions, named after
what they hold so that a later version of a standard supersedes them. Rules, agents and checks follow the
Antigravity and Amp conventions; `commands`, `context` and `domains` are ai-rulez's own. See
[.agents as a source](agents-source.md); `TestGenerateTranslatesTheSourceAndLeavesItAlone` and the `agents-source`
goldens back the claim that the standards' files are read and never rewritten. AGENTS.md defines no internal
structure, so reading it as one item per `##` heading (`agents_md_split = true`) is an ai-rulez convention, off by
default and covered by `TestAgentsMDSplitMakesOneItemPerHeading`. Nested `AGENTS.md` files are read as the standard
describes them, a file per directory applying to that directory's subtree (`TestNestedAGENTSMDIsScopedContext`).

#### Reading a status

A conformant status says the documents the tests produce validate. It does not say every possible configuration does:
the tests use representative projects (rules, context, skills, stdio and remote MCP servers). A schema accepting a
document also does not mean a given client will load it; the per-harness behaviour is in [harness traps](harness-traps.md).

#### CRUD Commands

AI-Rulez provides CRUD commands to programmatically modify your `.ai-rulez/` configuration. These commands allow you to create domains, add rules/context/skills/agents/commands, manage includes, and organize profiles.

##### Results, `--format json` and which project

Every command below prints its *result* on stdout and its confirmation sentence on stderr, so a script can
capture the result and `-q` only silences the sentence. `add`, `remove`, `edit` and `domain add|remove` print the
path they created, removed or rewrote, alone on a line (relative to the working directory when below it).
`profile`, `include` and `skill install|remove` change an entry in the config file, so they print nothing in
text mode.

`--format json` is accepted by `add`, `remove`, `edit`, `show`, `domain add|remove`, `profile add|remove|set-default`,
`include add|remove` and `skill install|remove`, and prints one versioned document
([schema](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Goldziher/ai-rulez/main/schema/change-result.schema.json)):

```json
{"schema_version": 1, "status": "created", "type": "rule", "name": "style", "domain": "backend", "path": ".ai-rulez/rules/style.md"}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| ----- | ------- |
| `status` | `created`, `removed` or `updated` |
| `type` | `rule`, `context`, `skill`, `agent`, `command`, `check`, `domain`, `profile`, `include`, `installed_skill` or `config` (`init`) |
| `name`, `domain` | The item and its domain (omitted for root content) |
| `path` | The file or directory created, removed or rewritten; for a profile, include or installed skill, the config file holding the entry (`config.local.toml` with `--local`) |
| `source`, `domains`, `default`, `local` | Present when they apply (an include's or skill's redacted source, a profile's domains and default flag, `--local`) |

`list` and `show` print their own documents. A failure under `--format json` is the standard error document.

The global `--config-dir <name>` (a directory below the working directory, or an absolute path) and `-C <dir>`
(a config directory such as `.ai-rulez` or `.agents`, or a file inside one such as `.agents/ai-rulez.toml`) select the project these commands act on, exactly as for `generate`.
Without them the directory is discovered: `.ai-rulez/`, then `.config/ai-rulez/`.

`ai-rulez add`, `remove`, `list`, `show`, `edit`, `domain`, `profile`, `include`, `skill` and `builtins` without a
subcommand print their help and exit 0; an unknown subcommand exits 1.

Names are file names: no `/`, no whitespace, no leading `.` or `-` and no trailing `.md` (the extension is added);
domains and skills use letters, digits, `_` and `-`. `--priority` is `critical|high|medium|low|minimal`;
`--targets` takes preset names, paths or globs and rejects an unknown word. `remove` checks that the item exists
before it asks for confirmation. `domain remove` refuses while a profile still lists the domain (remove the profile
first). A new skill without `--description` gets a placeholder that passes `validate`.

`add agent` and `add command` take `--domain`, `--description`, `--content` and
`--local`. `remove agent|command` and `list agents|commands` take the same flags as their rule/skill
counterparts.

`add check`, `remove check` and `list checks` manage code-review guidelines (see [Checks](checks.md));
they take `--domain` (and `--description`, `--content`, `--severity low|medium|high|critical`, `--tools a,b` and `--targets` for `add`; `--yes`/`-y` for `remove`) but have no `--local`.

`ai-rulez show <kind> <name>` prints the file as it is on disk (`--format json` adds the path). `ai-rulez edit <kind> <name>`
replaces the content atomically: `--content <text>` (use `-` for stdin), `--priority` and `--targets` for rules, context
and skills; for a check, content without frontmatter replaces only the body and `--description`, `--severity`,
`--tools` and `--targets` are set on its frontmatter. Both take `--domain`, and `--local` except for checks.

`edit` keeps what the file already declares: a rule, context file or skill rewritten with bare content keeps its
priority, targets, description and every other frontmatter key, and `--priority` or `--targets` change only that
field (the MCP `update_*` tools do the same). Content that starts with its own frontmatter replaces the whole file.
Content is never read, written or deleted through a symlink inside the configuration directory, and `index` and `log`
are reserved names: `index.md` and `log.md` are the listings `migrate okf` generates, so they are not rules, context
files or agents.

`ai-rulez list --placement [--profile <name>]` prints where every skill and command ends up (core or plugin-only),
the plugins that bundle it, and flags plugin-only items nothing makes reachable.

`ai-rulez skill update [name...]` re-resolves the named installed skills (all without names) and records the commit
and digest in `ai-rulez.lock`; it is `ai-rulez lock --kind skill`. A skill with a `version` range keeps a pin that still
satisfies it; [`ai-rulez update`](#update-command) moves range pins.

##### Include Management

Manage external rule sources (git repositories or local packages).

###### `ai-rulez include add <name> <source> [flags]`

Add a new include source to the configuration.

**Syntax:**

```bash
ai-rulez include add <name> <source> [flags]
```

**Arguments:**

- `<name>` (required): Unique identifier for this include
- `<source>` (required): Git URL (e.g., `https://github.com/org/repo`) or local path (e.g., `./packages/shared`)

**Flags:**

- `--path <dir>` (optional): Path within git repository where `.ai-rulez/` content is located
- `--ref <branch>` (optional): Git reference (branch, tag, commit). Defaults to the repository's default branch (`HEAD`), not necessarily `main`.
- `--include <types>` (optional): Comma-separated content types (default `rules,context,skills`): `rules,context,skills,agents,commands`
- `--merge-strategy <strategy>` (optional): Merge strategy: `local-override` (default), `include-override`, or `error`
- `--install-to <path>` (optional): Installation target path in `.ai-rulez/`
- `--local` (optional): Add the include to the machine-local `config.local.*` overlay instead of the shared config

A local source in the shared config must resolve inside the project, the same check the loader applies, so a path
outside it is refused when it is added (use `--local` for a path that leaves the project). A URL with a credential in
its userinfo (`https://user:token@host/...`) is refused: the credential would be written in clear into the committed
`config.toml`, so `include add` and `skill install` stop with the URL redacted and never write the secret. Keep the URL
free of secrets and authenticate with the git credential helper or the `AI_RULEZ_GIT_TOKEN` environment variable
(sent as a scoped git header, never stored); an SSH remote (`git@host:org/repo.git`) carries no credential. An existing
credentialed source is reported by `validate`/`scan` as `AR035` (see [Strict validation](strict-validation.md)).
`include remove` and `skill remove` edit `config.toml` directly without loading the project, so an include that keeps
the project from loading can always be removed.

**Examples:**

Add a git-based include:

```bash
ai-rulez include add corporate-rules https://github.com/myorg/shared-rules
```

Add with custom path and ref:

```bash
ai-rulez include add shared-patterns https://github.com/myorg/repo --path .ai-rulez --ref develop
```

Add local include:

```bash
ai-rulez include add backend-package ./packages/backend
```

###### `ai-rulez include remove <name> [flags]`

Remove an include source.

**Syntax:**

```bash
ai-rulez include remove <name> [flags]
```

**Arguments:**

- `<name>` (required): Include name to remove

**Flags:**

- `--yes` / `-y` (optional): Skip confirmation
- `--local` (optional): Remove through the `config.local.*` overlay. An include defined in the shared config is hidden on this machine with `remove = true`

**Examples:**

```bash
ai-rulez include remove corporate-rules
ai-rulez include remove shared-patterns --yes
```

###### `ai-rulez include list [flags]`

List all include sources.

**Syntax:**

```bash
ai-rulez include list [flags]
```

**Flags:**

- `--format text|json` (optional, default `text`): `json` prints JSON.

**Examples:**

```bash
ai-rulez include list
ai-rulez include list --format json
```
